comment_text.value:
qomplement.com ships today. It’s a native OS agent that learns complete GUI workflows from demonstration data, so you can ask for something open-ended—“Plan a weekend trip to SF, grab the cheapest round-trip and some cool tours”—and it handles vision, long-horizon reasoning, memory and UI control in one shot. There’s no prompt-tuning grind and no brittle script chain; each execution refines the model, so it keeps working even when the interface changes.

Instead of relying on predefined rules or manual orchestration, qomplement is trained end-to-end on full interaction traces that pair what the user sees with what the agent does, letting it generalise across apps. That removes the maintenance overhead and fragility that plague classic RPA stacks and most current “agent frameworks.” One model books flights, edits slides, reconciles spreadsheets, then gets smarter after every run.

We are very excited and believe this can open up a whole new world of applications.

We’re also live on Product Hunt today: https://www.producthunt.com/posts/qomplement?utm_source=othe...

- Kerim Taray

story_title.value: Qomplement: the first desktop AI agent

comment_text.value:
ooh, LLM Recsys alert! (we had an LLM Recsys track at ai.engineer last year). official announcement here: https://x.com/XEng/status/2013471689087086804

looks like this is the "for you" feed, once again shared without weights so we only have so much visibility into the actual influence of each trait.

"We have eliminated every single hand-engineered feature and most heuristics from the system. The Grok-based transformer does all the heavy lifting by understanding your engagement history (what you liked, replied to, shared, etc.) and using that to determine what content is relevant to you." aka it's a black box now.

the README is actually pretty nice, would recommend reading this. it doesnt look too different form Elon's original code review tweet/picture https://x.com/elonmusk/status/1593899029531803649?lang=en

sharing additonal notes while diving through the source: https://deepwiki.com/xai-org/x-algorithm

and a codemap of the signal generation pipeline: https://deepwiki.com/search/make-a-map-of-all-the-signals_3d...

- Phoenix (out of network) ranker seems to have all the interesting predictive ML work. it estimates P(favorite), P(reply), P(repost), P(quote), P(click), P(video_view), P(share), P(follow_author), P(not_interested), P(block_author), P(mute_author), P(report) independently and then the `WeightedScorer` combines them using configurable weights. there's an extra DiversityScore and OONScore to add some adjustments but again dont know the weights https://deepwiki.com/xai-org/x-algorithm/4.1-phoenix-candida... - other scores of interest: photo_expand_score, and dwell_score and dwell_time. share via copy, share, and share via dm are all obviously "super like" buttons.

- Two-Tower retrieval uses dot product similarity between user features/engagement (User Tower) and normalized embeddings for all items (Candidate Tower). but when you look into the code and considering that this is probably the most important model for recommendations quality.... it's maybe a little disappointing that its a 2 layer MLP? https://deepwiki.com/search/what-models-are-used-for-user_98...

- Grok-1 JAX transformer (https://github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm/blob/main/phoenix/REA...) uses special attention masking that prevents candidates from attending to each other during inference. Each candidate only attends to the user context (engagement history). This ensures a candidate's score is independent of which other candidates are in the batch, enabling score consistency and caching. nice image here https://github.com/xai-org/x-algorithm/blob/main/phoenix/REA...

- kind of nice usage of Rust traits to create a type safe data pipeline. look at this beautiful flow chart https://deepwiki.com/xai-org/x-algorithm/3-candidate-pipelin... and the "Field Ownership pattern" https://deepwiki.com/xai-org/x-algorithm/3.6-scorer-trait#fi...

- the ten pre-scoring filters are minorly interesting, nothing super surprising here apart from AgeFilter (https://deepwiki.com/xai-org/x-algorithm/4.6.1-agefilter) which I guess means beyond a certain max_age (1 day?) nothing ever shows up on For You. surprising to have a simple flat cutoff vs i guess the alternative of an exponential aging algorithm.

- videoduration hydrator explicitly prioritizes video duration (https://deepwiki.com/xai-org/x-algorithm/4.5.6-videoduration...) but we dont know in what direction... do you recommend shorter or longer videos? and why a hydrator for what is presumably a pretty static property?

open questions from me

1. how large is the production reranker? default param count is here https://deepwiki.com/search/how-many-params-is-the-transfo_c... but that gives no indication. the latency felt ultra high initially last year and seems to have come down some, what budget are we working with?

2. can we make the retrieval better? i dont have a tooon of confidence in the User Tower / Candidate Tower system - is this SOTA (it's probably not - see how youtube does codebook semantic id's https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LxQsQ3vZDqo&list=PLcfpQ4tk2k... )

3. no a/b testing / rollout infrastructure?

4. so many hydration subsystems - is this brittle?

comment_text.value:
I really like this approach. Nice job!

> We also plan to compile solved steps into micro‑policies. If you're running something like a RPA task or similar workflow as before, you can simply run the execution locally (with archon-mini running locally) and not have to worry about the planning. Over time, the planner is a background teacher, not a crutch.

Conceptually, I really like this - why re-do the work of reasoning about an already solved task? Just do it again. For some plausibly large majority of things, this could speed things up considerably.

> In the future we hope to run a streaming capture pipeline similar to Gemma 3. Consuming frames at 20–30 fps, emitting actions at 5–10 Hz, and verifying state on each commit.

I love targets like this. It makes you tune the architecture and abstractions to push the boundary of whats possible with a traditional agent loop.

The salience heat map compression is a great idea. I think you could take this a step further and tune a model so that it compresses an image into a textual semantic/interactive element hierarchy. This is effectively what browser-use is doing, just using javascript instead of a vision model.

This seems like a task that would benefit from narrow focus. I'm aware of the "Bitter Lesson," but my intuition seems to tell me that chaining together fit to purpose classification as an input to an intelligent planning system is the way to go.

story_title.value: Teaching GPT-5 to Use a Computer

I am still extremely bitter about how BioWare, in my opinion, ruined the dragon age franchise. While not "truly" turn based, dragon age origins and dragon age 2 had the spirit of it, and felt like a party-based tactical RPG. Then out of nowhere, the studio decided to abandon that with inquisition and turn it into an action/adventure style of game. I had never really been so bitterly disappointed with a game release.

After that I knew they were done. ME3 was the last good game they released, imo.

comment_text.value:
> I'm actually looking forward into owning an AVR and starting "simple"

I'm glad to hear that because reading your article, as each new sub-problem arose, I felt increasingly bad for you. We've all been in that spiraling sinkhole where every issue spawns two more :-).

I totally get the conceptual appeal of inexpensive, compact soundbar products: all-in-one, single input and wireless satellites. It seems great. It can even work as long as your sound-field expectations are modest AND you: 1) Happen to have a compatible room, 2) Commit to one incompatible, closed-ended product line, and 3) Nothing goes wrong because, as you discovered, these all-digital, integrated systems are largely opaque. While the initial cost can appear attractive, every dollar is locked into an inflexible system which can't grow beyond what its manufacturer offers and which may not be as good a fit in another room or reusable with other components.

I've never bought (or even considered) a soundbar, even in a context where it might have fit, been slightly cheaper or looked better with less effort - and I'm NOT an audiophile snob or insensitive to price. I'm an engineer so I see this like any other system design, an architectural choice with no perfect solutions, just different sets of trade-offs. Like many engineers, I've learned to value understanding systems from first principles, sometimes right down to the underlying physics of things. This often leads to some useful default assumptions, things which until proven otherwise, I broadly assume are probably directionally true. For example, when it comes to speakers, physical traits like surface area, volume and position matter. While it's true things like wave guides, linear arrays, digital signal processing and acoustic tricks (eg bouncing sound off ceiling/walls) can make smaller or poorly positioned speakers sound bigger or better than they should - it's still using cleverness to overcome a fundamental physical deficit.

Bottom line: all-other-things-equal, there's a point beyond which overcoming the deficits of smaller, fewer or poorly placed speakers yields diminishing returns - no matter what the marketing claims. So, I've always leaned toward investing my limited budgets in decent 'fundamentals' based on physics and economics. In audio, the physics means things like ensuring components have enough size and coverage to handle one of two generic residential sizes: small (bedroom/home office) and large (den/living room). Economically, it means investing in reuse so I'm not always starting over when I move/remodel and can repurpose older components into smaller or larger configs in the future.

Two examples: 1) The main speakers in my teenage daughter's bedroom were the best surrounds I could afford for our living room back when she was born. Getting slightly larger, better full-range surrounds back then paid off because they were good enough and flexible enough to have three lives (so far). 2) The first and cheapest AVR-ish amp I ever bought is now so old it has no digital inputs- but with a $15 BT/Wifi to RCA adapter, it's now driving the speakers above my garage workbench and it's a much better amp than I would ever have bought for our garage. If that AVR or those speakers had been integrated into an all-in-one box or limited to a proprietary ecosystem or digital protocol (wired or wireless) they'd probably already be in a landfill.

Another first principle is 'Ears are analog' and so are speakers and amplifier output stages. While digital formats can be great for storage and transport, all digital audio must become analog before you hear it. Your architectural choice is where in the signal chain it happens. Because home theater loudspeakers must be powered with a wire anyway AND because modern digital wireless transports are complex, opaque and not usually designed with real-time latency guarantees, an objective case can be made there are overall more advantages and less disadvantages to delivering home theater audio the last few feet on an inexpensive, universally compatible, broadly available analog wire. The delay is measured in nanoseconds with no latency, compression, pairing, interference, re-negotiation or channel hopping.

But these advantages do come with trade-offs. Instead of going wireless for satellites, I've had to get a little clever hiding wires, like running flat cables behind baseboard in a rental and, later, spending $70 on the right tools to run in-wall wires in my home. I think these trade-offs are worth it to get the reusability, flexibility, compatibility and transparency (for debugging).

It has a ton of semi-black box machinery around it, which can be taken apart with enough understanding of what you're doing. Despite Anthropic's benchmarks and claims, Claude was always the easiest to deceive or JB compared to e.g. GPT, which the RP community knows pretty well. They definitely improved it in 5.5 (due to distillation fears, ironically), but I'm not trusting their or anyone else's numbers this time either. These benchmarks always look good, and then there's someone routinely jailbreaking it layer through layer just for fun.

comment_text.value:
Actually, yes guidelines are actually that any prior statin prescription removes the need for CAC measurements. That includes those who are discovered to have statin intolerance, and thus requires out-of-pocket payment for any CAC.

I think the challenge here is that other than a CCTA there's no good way to estimate individual (as opposed to hereditary) ASCVD risk. Sure LDL, ApoB, Lp(a), and BP, are statistical proxies, but tell you little about the individual risk. CAC isn't much better, but if you've been taking EPA and VitK2 you have a much higher chance of more stable plaques, which are also more visible on CAC without much larger X-ray exposure and iodine contrast effects.

story_title.value: AI analysis of CT scans finds 42.9% of patients have coronary inflammation
